obligations.title: Records of Processing Activities (ROPA)
obligations.summary: Article 30 GDPR: Controllers (and processors) must maintain a written record of processing activities under their responsibility, including purposes, categories of data subjects and data, recipients, third-country transfers, retention schedules, and a general description of technical and organisational security measures. The 250-employee exemption in Article 30(5) is narrow (it does not apply where processing is not occasional, involves special categories, or is likely to result in a risk to data subjects) so most SMEs cannot rely on it.

why: The other live narration of the same finding, which failed differently and is worth its own row. Only the sentence below survives in ENT-247; the rest of that response was not kept, so this fixture is that sentence rather than a reconstruction of the whole. It is a non sequitur before it is a false statement of law, because whether a controller keeps a record does not determine its headcount, and no lexical check can see that. What a lexical check can see is that the model went near an exemption at all, which is the shape this case pins: the exemption is the corpus's to explain and the model has no business reasoning about it.

why: ENT-247's third acceptance criterion: a case whose correct answer requires the Article 30(5) exemption. A twelve-person firm whose processing is occasional is the organisation that exemption was written for, so a narrative asserting that the obligation binds everyone is wrong about this organisation and not merely loose. The weak response asserts it and is refused. The strong response does not decide the question at all, which is the right answer for a model to give: whether the exemption bites turns on three conditions, the corpus summary states them, and the renderer shows that summary beside the narrative. Before ENT-248 the weak response here was stored and shown to the customer as the explanation.
